intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that spermatogenic failure-103 (SPGF103) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the MEI1 gene on chromosome 22q13.

checks.claim: Spermatogenic failure-103 (SPGF103) is caused by homozygous or compound heterozygous mutation in the MEI1 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: Ben Khelifa and his team used WES technology to screen and identify a homozygous missense mutation c.C3307T (p.Arg1103Trp) in the MEI1 among two infertile brothers from a consanguineous Tunisian family
checks.explanation: This paper itself reports compound heterozygous MEI1 mutations. The homozygous mutation comes only from prior work it cites, and the paper does not use the SPGF103 designation.

checks.claim: The MEI1 gene is located on chromosome 22q13.
checks.evidence_quote: revealed the location of MEI1 in chromosome 22 (22q13.2)
checks.explanation: 22q13.2 lies within 22q13.

paragraphs.text: Spermatogenic failure-103 (SPGF103) is an autosomal recessive form of male infertility. Affected men have nonobstructive azoospermia, with spermatogenesis arrested at the spermatocyte stage, or cryptozoospermia (Chen et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2025).

checks.claim: Spermatogenic failure-103 (SPGF103) is an autosomal recessive form of male infertility.
checks.evidence_quote: The mutations were inherited from their parents, who were both single heterozygous carriers, indicating a recessive pattern of inheritance.
checks.explanation: The paper says recessive. Autosomal follows from MEI1's location on chromosome 22.

checks.claim: Some men affected with SPGF103 have nonobstructive azoospermia.
checks.evidence_quote: which was the first report of nonobstructive azoospermia (NOA) caused by MEI1 gene mutation due to meiotic arrest
checks.explanation: The paper cites earlier reports of NOA caused by MEI1 mutations.

checks.claim: In men with SPGF103 and nonobstructive azoospermia, spermatogenesis is arrested at the spermatocyte stage.
checks.evidence_quote: Testicular pathologic analysis and immunohistochemical staining revealed that spermatogenesis is arrested at spermatocyte stage
checks.explanation: Stated directly.

checks.claim: Some men affected with SPGF103 have cryptozoospermia.
checks.evidence_quote: we identified a new compound heterozygous mutation in MEI1 through WES and Sanger sequencing in two infertile brothers with cryptozoospermia
checks.explanation: Both brothers had cryptozoospermia.

paragraphs.text: Chen et al. (2023) reported 2 Chinese brothers with infertility. The proband was a 30-year-old man whose wife had not become pregnant during 5 years of unprotected intercourse. He had normal external genitalia, testicular volumes of about 12 ml on both sides, and no palpable abnormality of the spermatic cords or vasa deferentia. On three semen examinations, no spermatozoa were seen in the initial smear. In the centrifuged sediment, he had 0 to 1 sperm per high-power field (HPF), consistent with cryptozoospermia, and 10 to 15 spermatozoa were found in 20 HPF. Serum FSH, LH, testosterone, estradiol, prolactin, inhibin B, and anti-Mullerian hormone were normal. His karyotype was 46,XY, and he had no Y-chromosome AZF microdeletion. His brother had been infertile for 3 years of marriage. No sperm were seen in the brother's initial semen smears, but 0 to 1 motile sperm were occasionally seen after centrifugation, also consistent with cryptozoospermia. The brother's sex hormones, inhibin B, karyotype, and Y-chromosome microdeletion testing were normal. Their father had normal fertility.

The authors listed MEI1 among genes previously associated with infertility and presented these variants as candidate findings only, without functional or segregation studies.

paragraphs.text: In 2 Chinese brothers with SPGF103 and cryptozoospermia, Chen et al. (2023) found compound heterozygous mutations in the MEI1 gene: a splice site mutation downstream of exon 5 (c.529+5G-A) and a c.2071C-G transversion in exon 18 resulting in a gln691-to-glu (Q691E) substitution. The mutations were identified by whole-exome sequencing of the proband and confirmed by Sanger sequencing in both brothers. Neither variant was present in the ExAC or gnomAD databases. The father, who had normal fertility, was heterozygous for c.2071C-G, and the mother was heterozygous for c.529+5G-A. The splice site mutation was predicted to affect splicing, and several prediction programs predicted the missense mutation to be deleterious. Because the brothers had very few sperm and no testicular tissue was obtained, MEI1 mRNA and protein could not be assessed. The authors suggested that the combination of the 2 mutations might allow slight MEI1 expression and occasional completion of meiosis, which would explain cryptozoospermia rather than azoospermia.

checks.explanation: Compound heterozygous MEI1 mutations in two brothers with cryptozoospermia matches.

paragraphs.text: Using whole-exome sequencing, Zhang et al. (2023) identified biallelic deleterious variants in the MEI1 gene in 4 Chinese patients with nonobstructive azoospermia. In in vitro studies, a missense variant (c.186G-C) reduced MEI1 expression, and a frameshift variant (c.251delT) produced truncated MEI1 proteins. On the basis of bioinformatic analysis, another missense variant (c.1585T-A) was predicted to affect the interaction of MEI1 with its partners.

paragraphs.text: In a man with azoospermia and a woman with embryonic arrest from a consanguineous family, Liu et al. (2025) used whole-exome sequencing to identify a homozygous deletion of the whole of exon 19 of the MEI1 gene, which was confirmed by Sanger sequencing. Their mother was a heterozygous carrier. Amplification and sequencing of cDNA confirmed loss of the exon, and exon 19 expression was almost undetectable in the patients. In HEK293T cells, the deletion resulted in a truncated MEI1 protein, consistent with the predicted premature termination in exon 20.

checks.explanation: Variant, exon and protein change match; found in the two brothers with cryptozoospermia.

checks.claim: In the brothers reported by Chen et al. (2023), MEI1 Q691E was compound heterozygous with the splice site mutation c.529+5G-A.
checks.evidence_quote: A novel compound heterozygous mutation was identified in the meiotic double-stranded break formation protein 1 (MEI1) gene (Online Mendelian Inheritance in Man [OMIM]: 608797), including the missense mutation c.2071C>G (p.Gln691Glu) located in exon 18 and the splicing mutation c.529+5G>A
checks.explanation: Q691E is compound heterozygous with the splice variant.

checks.claim: The fertile father of the brothers reported by Chen et al. (2023) was heterozygous for MEI1 Q691E.
checks.evidence_quote: only their father carried the c.2071C>G heterozygous mutation and had normal fertility
checks.explanation: Fertile father heterozygous for Q691E matches.

checks.claim: The MEI1 Q691E variant was absent from ExAC and gnomAD.
checks.evidence_quote: These two variants have not been included in ExAC or gnomAD thus far.
checks.explanation: Absent from ExAC and gnomAD matches.

checks.claim: MutationTaster, SIFT, FATHMM, and M-CAP all predicted MEI1 Q691E to be deleterious.
checks.evidence_quote: Prediction software such as MutationTaster, SIFT, Functional Analysis through Hidden Markov Models (FATHMM), and M-CAP all predicted the deleteriousness of the missense mutation c.2071C>G.
checks.explanation: The four named programs all predicted it deleterious.

paragraphs.text: In a man with azoospermia and a woman with embryonic arrest from a consanguineous family, Liu et al. (2025) identified a homozygous deletion of the whole of exon 19 of the MEI1 gene. It was found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing, and their mother was a heterozygous carrier. In the patients, exon 19 expression was almost undetectable. In HEK293T cells, the deletion produced a truncated MEI1 protein, consistent with predicted premature termination in exon 20.

checks.claim: Liu et al. (2025) identified a homozygous deletion of the whole of exon 19 of MEI1 in a man with azoospermia and a woman with embryonic arrest from a consanguineous family.
checks.evidence_quote: The novel homozygous whole exon deletion of exon 19 in MEI1 was detected by WES.

checks.claim: The MEI1 exon 19 deletion was found by whole-exome sequencing and confirmed by Sanger sequencing.
checks.evidence_quote: Mutations were detected by whole-exome sequencing (WES) and confirmed by Sanger sequencing.

checks.claim: The mother of the patients reported by Liu et al. (2025) was a heterozygous carrier of the MEI1 exon 19 deletion.
checks.evidence_quote: their mother is a heterozygous carrier of this whole exon deletion.

checks.claim: MEI1 exon 19 expression was almost undetectable in the patients reported by Liu et al. (2025).
checks.evidence_quote: Quantitative expression revealed that the deletion result in almost no detectable expression of MEI1 Exon 19 in patients

checks.claim: In HEK293T cells, the MEI1 exon 19 deletion produced a truncated MEI1 protein.
checks.evidence_quote: Western blotting revealed that the whole exon deletion in MEI1 result in production of truncated MEI1 protein
checks.explanation: Functional characterization was done by transfection in HEK293T cells.

checks.claim: The truncated MEI1 protein from the exon 19 deletion was consistent with predicted premature termination in exon 20.
checks.evidence_quote: result in production of truncated MEI1 protein, corresponding to the predicted premature termination at Exon 20 of MEI1.

agent.process_note: Read all five papers in full: Chen 2023 and Malcher 2022 as full texts; Nguyen 2018, Zhang 2023 and Liu 2025 as abstracts only. Searched Malcher for MEI1 and found one patient with compound heterozygous variants; that patient's histologic phenotype is not given in the extracted text. Because Zhang 2023 is abstract-only, its protein changes and per-patient zygosity were not available, so its variants were not made into allelic-variant entries. Nguyen 2018 deals with MEI1 in women with recurrent hydatidiform moles and in female mice; only the mouse finding was used, as an animal model. The gene's MIM number was left out because no reference data were supplied. The chromosome location (22q13.2) comes from Chen 2023 and Malcher 2022.
